text: Michael John Creutz, born on November 24, 1944, in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is an American theoretical physicist at Brookhaven National Laboratory, specializing in lattice gauge theory and computational physics. His father, Edward Creutz, was also a physicist and was involved in the Manhattan Project at the time of Michael's birth. Creutz earned his bachelor's degree in physics with honor from Caltech in 1966 and completed his graduate studies at Stanford University under a NSF Graduate Fellowship, graduating in 1970. His thesis was conducted at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, with Sidney Drell as his adviser. Following graduation, he served as a research associate at SLAC before joining the Center for Theoretical Physics at the University of Maryland, College Park, as a fellow from 1970 to 1972. In 1972, he joined the High Energy Theory Group at Brookhaven National Laboratory, becoming a senior physicist in 1985 and serving as group leader from 1984 to 1987. In 2003, he became an adjunct professor at the C. N. Yang Institute for Theoretical Physics at Stony Brook University. His research covers various areas in particle physics and mathematical physics, but he is best known for his work on lattice QCD. His 1983 textbook, *Quarks, Gluons, and Lattices*, was the first full-length textbook on lattice QCD and is regarded as a classic in the field. Creutz is a fellow of the American Physical Society and received the Aneesur Rahman Prize for Computational Physics in 2000 "for first demonstrating that properties of QCD could be computed numerically on the lattice through Monte Carlo methods, and for numerous contributions to the field thereafter." In 2009, he was awarded the Humboldt Research Award.
